newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Airlines ready for fresh talks on HK airport fees.
newsitem.headline: Airlines ready for fresh talks on HK airport fees.

text.p: Airline officials are due to meet Hong Kong's Airport Authority over the next two days for talks on how much they will have to pay to use Hong Kong's new airport.
The talks on April 24 and 25 are the sixth round of negotiations which have fuelled an increasing controversy.

Industry sources said the latest indications from the authority are that Boeing 747 landing fees will double from HK$31,426 at Kai Tak to HK$66,877 at Chek Lap Kok while for a Boeing 737 charges would rise from HK$8,502 to HK$15,943.

Airlines and representative bodies such as the Orient Airlines Association -- now renamed the Association of Asia Pacific Airlines -- said they are dismayed at Chek Lap Kok becoming one of the world's most expensive airports.

Stanley Hui, chief executive officer at Hong Kong Dragon Airlines which would base its regional network at Chek Lap Kok, warned some flights, particularly short-haul, would have to be terminated as they would become uneconomic.
Hui said he hoped the International Air Transport Association (IATA) Users Charges Board would be able to "talk down" the charges during this week.
"If fees are too expensive then someone will have to pay - either the airlines or the consumer I don't know," he told reporters on Monday as Dragonair prepared to launch a new service to Chongqing.

"The additional landing charges make the economics look terrible and airlines may be forced to make a commercial decision and suspend marginal services. Especially on short haul services, air fares are very low and when you look at the additional cost per seat it is very significant," Hui said.
"As long as we continue talking I am sure we will find a solution," Hui added.
Gilbert Chow, Hong Kong general manager for Northwest Airlines and a representative of the IATA User Charges Board described the next round of talks as "long and challenging."

In an increasing battle of words, the authority has replied to the mounting criticism from airlines and said the new airport will provide far greater value for money than at the existing Kai Tak airport.
It said the new charges have been carefully calculated to be fair, reasonable, simple, non-discriminatory and competitive.
